questions.q: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis?
questions.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptides.

questions.q: Which feature is found in prokaryotic cells?
questions.why: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles; their ribosomes are 70S.

questions.q: The resolution of a light microscope is limited by…
questions.why: Resolution is about half the wavelength used; electrons have much shorter wavelengths.

questions.q: An eyepiece graticule must be calibrated using…
questions.why: The stage micrometer's known divisions give the value of each graticule unit at that magnification.

questions.q: Which structure is found in the cytoplasm of prokaryotic cells?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): two thirds of weaker candidates chose endoplasmic reticulum; prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles.

questions.q: Which organelle contains hydrolytic enzymes responsible for breaking down cellular waste and ingested pathogens?
questions.why: Lysosomes maintain an acidic interior with acid hydrolases that digest macromolecules, old organelles, and engulfed foreign matter.

long.q: In an electron micrograph a mitochondrion measures 18 mm. Its actual length is 3 µm. Calculate the magnification of the image.
scheme: A1: magnification = 18 000 ÷ 3 = × 6000

long.q: Describe the roles of the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi body in the production and secretion of an extracellular enzyme.
scheme: B1: ribosomes on the rough ER synthesise the polypeptide (translation)
B1: the polypeptide enters the RER lumen, where it folds, and is carried in vesicles to the Golgi body
B1: the Golgi body modifies and packages the protein (e.g. adds carbohydrate to form a glycoprotein) into secretory vesicles
B1: secretory vesicles move to and fuse with the cell surface membrane, releasing the enzyme by exocytosis

long.q: State four structural differences between a typical prokaryotic cell and a typical animal cell.
scheme: B1: prokaryote has no nucleus or nuclear envelope; its DNA lies free in the cytoplasm
B1: prokaryotic DNA is circular and not associated with histone proteins (animal DNA is linear, with histones)
B1: prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes; animal cells have 80S ribosomes in the cytoplasm
B1: prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or ER, but have a peptidoglycan cell wall (and may have plasmids), which animal cells lack

long.q: An eyepiece graticule is calibrated with a stage micrometer whose divisions are each 10 µm apart. 40 eyepiece divisions line up exactly with 12 stage micrometer divisions. A cell spans 25 eyepiece divisions. Calculate the actual length of the cell.
scheme: B1: 12 stage micrometer divisions = 12 × 10 = 120 µm
M1: one eyepiece division = 120 ÷ 40 = 3.0 µm
A1: length of cell = 25 × 3.0 = 75 µm

long.q: Explain why ribosomes can be seen with an electron microscope but not with a light microscope.
scheme: B1: electrons have a much shorter wavelength than visible light
B1: so the electron microscope has a much higher resolution (about 0.5 nm compared with about 200 nm)
B1: ribosomes (about 20–25 nm across) are smaller than the resolution limit of the light microscope, so they cannot be distinguished, but they can be with electrons

questions.q: Which bond joins two α-glucose molecules in maltose?
questions.why: A condensation reaction forms an α-1,4 glycosidic bond.

questions.q: What gives cellulose its strength?
o: Hydrogen bonds between parallel chains of β-glucose forming microfibrils
questions.why: Alternate β-glucose units are inverted, giving straight chains that hydrogen-bond together.

questions.q: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids?
questions.why: The primary structure determines how the chain folds.

questions.q: Why is water a good solvent?
o: It is polar, so ions and polar molecules dissolve
questions.why: Its δ+ and δ− regions surround charged and polar particles.

questions.q: Which statement about cellulose is correct?
o: It is an unbranched chain of β-glucose, held in microfibrils by hydrogen bonds
It is a branched chain of α-glucose
Its chains coil into a helix
It is a polymer of fructose
questions.why: Examiners (2023): many thought cellulose is branched or coils into a helix; that describes starch (amylopectin and amylose).

questions.q: Which statement about triglycerides is correct?
o: They are non-polar and insoluble in water
questions.why: Examiners (2023): half of weaker candidates believed triglycerides are polar.

questions.q: Which bond forms between the glycerol molecule and fatty acids in a triglyceride?
questions.why: Condensation reactions between each –OH group of glycerol and the –COOH group of a fatty acid produce ester bonds with the elimination of water.

long.q: Describe the structure of cellulose and explain how it suits its role in plant cell walls.
scheme: B1: β-glucose monomers joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds, alternate ones rotated 180°
B1: long straight chains held together by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils
B1: giving high tensile strength, so the wall resists bursting when the cell is turgid

long.q: Describe how a peptide bond is formed between two amino acids.
scheme: B1: a condensation reaction
B1: between the amine group (–NH₂) of one amino acid and the carboxyl group (–COOH) of the other
B1: a molecule of water is removed and a C–N (peptide) bond forms, giving a dipeptide

long.q: Explain how the structure of a triglyceride makes it suitable as an energy store.
scheme: B1: the fatty acid chains contain many C–H bonds, so oxidation releases a lot of energy (about twice as much per gram as carbohydrate)
B1: triglycerides are non-polar and insoluble in water, so they do not affect the water potential of cells
B1: they are compact (low mass for the energy stored), useful for animals that move or for seeds

long.q: Describe how you could use the Benedict's test to compare the concentrations of reducing sugar in two solutions.
scheme: B1: add the same volume of each solution to the same volume of Benedict's solution (in excess)
B1: heat in a water bath at about 80–100 °C for the same length of time
B1: colour changes from blue through green, yellow and orange to brick-red; the more red / more precipitate, the higher the concentration
B1: compare against standards of known concentration, or use a colorimeter / filter and dry the precipitate for a more objective comparison

long.q: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other. Explain how this gives water two properties that are important to living organisms.
scheme: B1: water is polar (δ– oxygen, δ+ hydrogens), so hydrogen bonds form between molecules
B1: high specific heat capacity: much energy is needed to break hydrogen bonds before temperature rises
B1: so the temperature of cells and aquatic habitats stays fairly stable
B1: second property with importance, e.g. high latent heat of vaporisation so sweating / transpiration cools, or solvent for polar substances and ions so transport and reactions happen in solution

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor…
o: binds to the active site, competing with the substrate
binds elsewhere and changes the active site
questions.why: Raising substrate concentration can overcome it; Vmax is unchanged.

questions.q: A low Km means the enzyme has…
questions.why: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax; low Km means it reaches it at low concentration.

questions.q: Why are immobilised enzymes useful?
o: They work faster than free enzymes always
They can be reused and are more stable, and the product isn't contaminated
questions.why: Fixing enzymes in beads makes separation and reuse easy.

questions.q: In an enzyme-catalysed reaction, the rate rises as substrate concentration increases but then levels off. Why does it level off?
o: The substrate has been used up
The enzyme has been denatured by the extra substrate
All the active sites are occupied at any moment, so enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor
The product acts as a competitive inhibitor
questions.why: At high substrate concentration the enzyme is saturated: adding more substrate cannot form enzyme–substrate complexes any faster, so the rate reaches Vmax.

questions.q: How does a competitive inhibitor affect Vmax and Km?
questions.why: A high enough substrate concentration out-competes the inhibitor, so Vmax can still be reached; but more substrate is needed to reach half Vmax, so Km rises.

long.q: Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor affects the Vmax and the Michaelis–Menten constant (Km) of an enzyme.
scheme: B1: it binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site)
B1: changing the shape of the active site, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form
B1: Vmax is lower; adding more substrate does not overcome it
B1: Km is unchanged (the affinity of the remaining active enzymes is the same)

long.q: Explain why the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction decreases when the temperature rises above the optimum.
scheme: B1: increased kinetic energy makes the enzyme molecule vibrate, breaking hydrogen and ionic bonds
B1: the tertiary structure changes, so the shape of the active site changes (the enzyme is denatured)
B1: the substrate no longer fits / is not complementary, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form

long.q: In an investigation of catalase, 18 cm³ of oxygen was collected in 2 minutes 30 seconds. Calculate the mean rate of oxygen production in cm³ s⁻¹.
scheme: M1: 2 minutes 30 seconds = 150 s
A1: rate = 18 ÷ 150 = 0.12 cm³ s⁻¹

long.q: Explain the induced-fit hypothesis of enzyme action.
scheme: B1: the active site is not exactly complementary to the substrate at first
B1: as the substrate binds, the active site changes shape slightly to fit it more closely
B1: this puts strain on bonds in the substrate, lowering the activation energy of the reaction

long.q: Explain two advantages of using an enzyme immobilised in alginate beads rather than the same enzyme free in solution.
scheme: B1: the enzyme can be easily separated from the product
B1: so the product is not contaminated and the enzyme can be reused, saving cost
B1: immobilised enzymes are more stable / less easily denatured
B1: so they work over a wider range of temperature or pH (and allow a continuous process)

questions.q: In the fluid mosaic model, what makes the membrane fluid?
o: Phospholipids that move within the layer
questions.why: Phospholipids move laterally; cholesterol regulates fluidity.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion uses…
o: channel or carrier proteins, down a concentration gradient
questions.why: It is passive, but needs proteins for polar or charged molecules.

questions.q: Water potential of pure water is…
questions.why: Ψ of pure water is 0 kPa; solutes make it negative.

questions.q: Where is cholesterol found in a cell surface membrane?
o: Between the phospholipid tails, with its OH group near the heads
questions.why: Examiners (2023): three fifths of weaker candidates thought cholesterol only occurs between the heads.

questions.q: Two neighbouring plant cells have water potentials of −400 kPa (cell A) and −700 kPa (cell B). What happens?
o: Water moves from B to A, because B has more solute
Water moves from A to B, down the water potential gradient
There is no net movement, because both values are negative
Water moves from B to A, because B has the lower water potential
questions.why: Water moves by osmosis from a higher (less negative) to a lower (more negative) water potential: −400 kPa is higher than −700 kPa, so water moves from A into B.

long.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. Explain, in terms of water potential, what happens to the cell.
scheme: B1: pure water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the cell (0 kPa)
B1: water moves into the cell by osmosis, down the water potential gradient, through the partially permeable membrane
B1: the cell becomes turgid; the cell wall stops it bursting

long.q: Describe the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure.
scheme: B1: a phospholipid bilayer, with hydrophilic phosphate heads facing outwards and hydrophobic fatty acid tails facing inwards
B1: proteins scattered through it like a mosaic: intrinsic (spanning the bilayer, e.g. channels and carriers) and extrinsic
B1: phospholipids and many proteins move laterally, so the membrane is fluid
B1: cholesterol between phospholipids regulates fluidity; glycoproteins and glycolipids on the outer surface act in cell recognition / as receptors

long.q: Compare active transport with facilitated diffusion.
scheme: B1: both use transport proteins in the membrane and are specific to particular molecules or ions
B1: active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient; facilitated diffusion only down the gradient
B1: active transport needs energy from ATP (from respiration); facilitated diffusion is passive
B1: active transport uses carrier proteins that change shape; facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins

long.q: Two cubes of agar contain an indicator that changes colour when acid diffuses in. One cube has sides of 2 cm and the other has sides of 1 cm. Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of each cube and explain why the larger cube takes longer to change colour completely.
scheme: B1: 2 cm cube: surface area 24 cm², volume 8 cm³, ratio 3 : 1
B1: 1 cm cube: surface area 6 cm², volume 1 cm³, ratio 6 : 1
B1: the larger cube has less surface area per unit volume through which acid can enter
B1: and the distance from the surface to the centre is greater, so diffusion takes longer

long.q: Outline how a water-soluble hormone that cannot cross the cell surface membrane brings about a response inside its target cell.
scheme: B1: the hormone binds to a specific receptor (with a complementary shape) on the outer surface of the cell surface membrane
B1: the receptor changes shape and activates a signalling pathway inside the cell, e.g. a G protein and a second messenger such as cyclic AMP
B1: the signal is amplified by a cascade of enzyme activations, producing the response (e.g. activating an enzyme or changing gene expression)

questions.q: In which stage do chromosomes line up on the equator?
questions.why: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres and align chromosomes at metaphase.

questions.q: When is DNA replicated?
questions.why: DNA synthesis happens in the S phase before mitosis.

questions.q: What is the role of telomeres?
o: Protect chromosome ends from losing genes during replication
questions.why: Repeated non-coding sequences are lost instead of genes.

questions.q: Which statement about mitosis is correct?
o: Daughter cells are the same size as the parent
Semi-conservative DNA replication happens during mitosis
The nuclear envelope breaks down during prophase
questions.why: Examiners (2023): candidates thought DNA replication is part of mitosis (it is in interphase) or forgot the nuclear envelope breaks down in prophase.

questions.q: At which stage of mitosis do sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the spindle?
questions.why: During anaphase, cohesin proteins break down and kinetochore spindle fibres pull separated sister chromatids to opposite poles.

long.q: Describe the behaviour of the chromosomes during the four stages of mitosis.
scheme: B1: prophase: chromosomes condense and become visible as two sister chromatids joined at the centromere; the nuclear envelope breaks down
B1: metaphase: chromosomes line up on the equator, attached by their centromeres to spindle fibres
B1: anaphase: centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles by the shortening spindle fibres
B1: telophase: chromatids reach the poles, uncoil, and a nuclear envelope reforms around each set

long.q: Explain the significance of mitosis in living organisms.
scheme: B1: it produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other and to the parent, with the same chromosome number
B1: so it is used for growth and for the repair or replacement of damaged and worn-out cells
B1: and for asexual reproduction, and clonal expansion of lymphocytes in an immune response

long.q: Explain the role of telomeres in the mitotic cell cycle.
scheme: B1: telomeres are repeated non-coding base sequences at the ends of chromosomes
B1: DNA polymerase cannot copy the very end of a DNA strand, so a little is lost at each replication
B1: the telomere is shortened instead of genes being lost, so the chromosome's genetic information is protected (telomerase rebuilds telomeres in stem cells)

long.q: In a root tip squash, 32 of 400 cells counted were in mitosis. The whole cell cycle in this tissue takes 20 hours. Assuming time in a stage is proportional to the number of cells in it, estimate the time spent in mitosis, in minutes.
scheme: M1: fraction of cells in mitosis = 32 ÷ 400 = 0.08
M1: time in mitosis = 0.08 × 20 h = 1.6 h
A1: 1.6 × 60 = 96 minutes

long.q: Explain how mutations can lead to the formation of a tumour.
scheme: B1: mutations occur in genes that control the cell cycle (proto-oncogenes become oncogenes, or tumour suppressor genes stop working)
B1: so the cell divides repeatedly by mitosis without control
B1: producing a mass of cells (a tumour), which may spread to other tissues (metastasis)

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because…
o: each new molecule has one original strand and one new strand
it happens in half the cells
questions.why: Shown by the Meselson–Stahl experiment.

questions.q: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments?
questions.why: Ligase seals the gaps in the lagging strand.

questions.q: During translation, tRNA anticodons pair with…
questions.why: Complementary base pairing places the right amino acid.

questions.q: A substitution mutation may have no effect because…
o: the genetic code is degenerate (several codons per amino acid)
questions.why: A different codon can still code for the same amino acid.

questions.q: Which sugar is found in ATP?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): nearly three fifths of weaker candidates said deoxyribose.

questions.q: What enzyme synthesises an mRNA transcript from a DNA template strand during transcription?
questions.why: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter, unwinds the helix, and synthesises complementary pre-mRNA from 5' to 3'.

long.q: Describe how DNA replicates semi-conservatively.
scheme: B1: hydrogen bonds between bases break and the double helix unwinds (helicase)
B1: each strand acts as a template
B1: free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G)
B1: DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides, so each new molecule has one old strand and one new strand

long.q: Describe the process of transcription.
scheme: B1: the DNA double helix unwinds and hydrogen bonds between bases break at the gene
B1: one strand (the template strand) is used
B1: free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A with U, C with G)
B1: RNA polymerase joins them to form mRNA, which leaves the nucleus through a nuclear pore

long.q: Describe how a polypeptide is assembled during translation.
scheme: B1: mRNA attaches to a ribosome in the cytoplasm
B1: each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon
B1: tRNA anticodons pair with complementary mRNA codons, two at a time on the ribosome
B1: a peptide bond forms between adjacent amino acids
B1: the ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time until a stop codon is reached

long.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate. Explain what this means and how it allows some base substitution mutations to have no effect on the protein.
scheme: B1: most amino acids are coded for by more than one triplet (codon)
B1: a substitution may change a codon into another codon for the same amino acid
B1: so the primary structure, and therefore the protein, is unchanged (a silent mutation)

long.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 22% adenine. Calculate the percentage of guanine in the sample.
scheme: M1: A pairs with T, so thymine is also 22% and A + T = 44%
A1: G + C = 56%, and G = C, so guanine = 28%

questions.q: What drives water up the xylem?
o: Transpiration pull, with cohesion and adhesion
questions.why: Evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water up.

questions.q: Sucrose is loaded into phloem sieve tubes by…
o: co-transport with H⁺ via companion cells
questions.why: Companion cells pump H⁺ out; sucrose re-enters with H⁺ through co-transporters.

questions.q: Xerophytes reduce water loss by…
o: sunken stomata, rolled leaves and thick cuticles
questions.why: These trap humid air and reduce the surface exposed.

questions.q: Water moving through the apoplast pathway in a root:
o: moves only by osmosis through membranes
moves by mass flow through cell walls
questions.why: Examiners (2023): over half of candidates said the apoplast pathway does not involve mass flow.

questions.q: What causes the mass flow of phloem sap from a source to a sink?
o: Active pumping of sap by the companion cells along the whole sieve tube
A hydrostatic pressure gradient: sucrose loading at the source lowers water potential so water enters, and unloading at the sink has the opposite effect
questions.why: Water following sucrose by osmosis raises hydrostatic pressure at the source and lowers it at the sink, so sap flows down the pressure gradient, in either direction depending on where sources and sinks are.

long.q: Explain how water moves up the xylem from the roots to the leaves.
scheme: B1: water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out of the stomata (transpiration)
B1: this lowers the hydrostatic pressure at the top of the xylem, creating tension
B1: water molecules are held together by hydrogen bonds (cohesion) so a continuous column is pulled up
B1: adhesion of water to the lignified xylem walls also helps; mass flow from high to low pressure

long.q: Describe the pathways water takes across the root cortex and explain the role of the Casparian strip.
scheme: B1: apoplast pathway: water moves through the cell walls and spaces between cells
B1: symplast pathway: water moves through the cytoplasm, passing between cells via plasmodesmata
B1: at the endodermis the Casparian strip, made of suberin, blocks the apoplast pathway
B1: so water must enter the cytoplasm, crossing a membrane, which lets the plant control which ions enter the xylem

long.q: Explain how sucrose is transported from a source to a sink in the phloem.
scheme: B1: companion cells pump H⁺ out using ATP, and H⁺ re-enters with sucrose through cotransporter proteins (active loading)
B1: sucrose moves into the sieve tube elements, lowering their water potential
B1: water enters from the xylem by osmosis, raising the hydrostatic pressure at the source
B1: at the sink sucrose is removed (used or stored), water leaves, so pressure is lower
B1: the sap moves by mass flow from high to low pressure, through the sieve plates

long.q: Explain how two features of the leaves of a xerophyte reduce water loss.
scheme: B1: a first feature, e.g. stomata sunken in pits or a rolled leaf with hairs
B1: traps humid air near the stomata, reducing the water potential gradient, so less water diffuses out
B1: a second feature, e.g. a thick waxy cuticle, or fewer stomata, or small / needle-shaped leaves
B1: explanation, e.g. the cuticle is waterproof so less evaporation through the epidermis, or a smaller surface area for water loss

long.q: In a potometer the air bubble moves 45 mm along a capillary tube of radius 0.50 mm in 5.0 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. (Volume of a cylinder = πr²l.)
scheme: M1: cross-sectional area = π × 0.50² = 0.785 mm²
A1: rate = 35.3 ÷ 5.0 = 7.1 mm³ min⁻¹

questions.q: The Bohr effect means that high CO₂ concentration…
questions.why: Oxygen is released more readily where respiration is high.

questions.q: What starts each heartbeat?
questions.why: The SAN starts a wave of excitation; the AVN delays it before the ventricles contract.

questions.q: Tissue fluid forms because at the arterial end of a capillary…
o: hydrostatic pressure is greater than the osmotic pull
questions.why: Fluid is forced out; most returns at the venous end.

questions.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
o: Hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻), mostly in the plasma
Carbonic acid molecules in the plasma
questions.why: Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells converts CO₂ and water to H₂CO₃, which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; the HCO₃⁻ diffuses into the plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ (the chloride shift).

questions.q: During the cardiac cycle, what causes the atrioventricular valves to close?
o: Pressure in the atria rises above pressure in the ventricles
Pressure in the ventricles rises above pressure in the atria as the ventricles contract
Pressure in the ventricles falls below pressure in the aorta
An impulse from the SAN contracts the valve tissue
questions.why: Valves open and close passively because of pressure differences; when ventricular pressure exceeds atrial pressure, blood pushes the AV valve flaps shut, preventing backflow into the atria.

long.q: Explain the Bohr shift and why it is useful in actively respiring tissues.
scheme: B1: high carbon dioxide concentration lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (curve shifts right)
B1: CO₂ forms carbonic acid, and H⁺ ions bind to haemoglobin forming haemoglobinic acid
B1: so more oxygen is released (unloaded) where it is needed for respiration

long.q: Explain how the heartbeat is initiated and coordinated.
scheme: B1: the sinoatrial node (SAN) in the wall of the right atrium generates a wave of electrical excitation (it is the pacemaker)
B1: the wave spreads across both atria, which contract (atrial systole)
B1: a layer of non-conducting tissue stops it passing directly to the ventricles; it reaches the atrioventricular node (AVN)
B1: the AVN delays the impulse (about 0.1 s) so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract
B1: the impulse passes down the Purkyne tissue in the septum to the apex, so the ventricles contract from the bottom upwards

long.q: Explain how the structure of the wall of an artery is related to its function.
scheme: B1: thick layer of elastic fibres stretches as blood surges in and recoils, evening out the pressure / maintaining flow
B1: thick wall (with collagen and smooth muscle) withstands high pressure without bursting
B1: smooth endothelium lining the narrow lumen reduces friction, keeping blood at high pressure

long.q: Explain how tissue fluid is formed and how most of it is returned to the blood.
scheme: B1: at the arterial end of a capillary the hydrostatic pressure of the blood is high
B1: fluid (water and small solutes such as glucose and ions) is forced out through gaps in the capillary wall; plasma proteins and cells are too large and stay in
B1: at the venous end the hydrostatic pressure is lower and the plasma proteins give the blood a lower water potential than the tissue fluid
B1: so water moves back in by osmosis; the excess drains into lymph vessels

long.q: Describe how most of the carbon dioxide produced by respiring cells is carried in the blood.
scheme: B1: carbon dioxide diffuses into red blood cells
B1: carbonic anhydrase catalyses CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃ (carbonic acid)
B1: carbonic acid dissociates into H⁺ and hydrogencarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻)
B1: HCO₃⁻ diffuses out into the plasma, where most is carried, and Cl⁻ moves in (the chloride shift)
B1: H⁺ ions combine with haemoglobin to form haemoglobinic acid, which buffers the blood

questions.q: What is the role of cartilage in the trachea?
questions.why: C-shaped rings stop the trachea collapsing.

questions.q: Goblet cells…
questions.why: Cilia then sweep the mucus upwards.

questions.q: Which tissue lines the trachea and bronchi and produces mucus?
questions.why: Examiners (2023): 'endothelium' was a wrong choice: that term is only used for blood vessels.

questions.q: Which feature of the alveoli most directly shortens the diffusion distance for oxygen?
o: A surfactant that coats their inner surface
The large number of alveoli in each lung
Walls made of a single layer of thin, flattened (squamous) epithelial cells next to capillary walls
questions.why: Thin squamous epithelium and thin capillary walls mean oxygen crosses only about two cells; the large number of alveoli increases surface area rather than shortening the distance.

questions.q: What is the role of elastic fibres in the walls of the alveoli?
o: They stretch during inhalation and recoil during exhalation, helping to push air out
They contract to close the airways
They keep the alveoli permanently open, like cartilage
questions.why: Elastic fibres stretch as the alveoli fill and then recoil, helping to expel air; they are passive, unlike smooth muscle, and do not hold airways open as cartilage does.

long.q: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange.
scheme: B1: very large number of alveoli gives a large total surface area
B1: walls are one cell thick (squamous epithelium) next to thin capillary walls, so the diffusion distance is short
B1: a dense capillary network carries oxygenated blood away, maintaining a steep concentration gradient
B1: ventilation replaces alveolar air, also maintaining the gradient (elastic fibres help expel air)

long.q: Explain how goblet cells and ciliated epithelial cells work together to protect the gas exchange surface.
scheme: B1: goblet cells secrete mucus
B1: the mucus traps dust, pollen and pathogens in the inhaled air
B1: cilia beat in a coordinated way to move the mucus up the airways to the throat, where it is swallowed

long.q: State the role in the airways of each of these tissues: cartilage, smooth muscle, elastic fibres.
scheme: B1: cartilage supports the trachea and bronchi and keeps them open when air pressure inside falls during inspiration
B1: smooth muscle contracts or relaxes to change the diameter of the airways, controlling air flow
B1: elastic fibres stretch when we breathe in and recoil when we breathe out, helping to push air out of the alveoli

long.q: In a lung disease the walls between neighbouring alveoli break down, forming fewer, larger air spaces, and elastic fibres are lost. Explain why the person absorbs less oxygen.
scheme: B1: fewer, larger spaces have a smaller total surface area for diffusion
B1: loss of elastic fibres means the alveoli do not recoil, so less stale air is expelled
B1: the concentration gradient of oxygen between the air and the blood is smaller, so less oxygen diffuses into the blood

long.q: Compare the distribution of cartilage, goblet cells and smooth muscle in the trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.
scheme: B1: cartilage is present as C-shaped rings in the trachea and as irregular plates in the bronchi
B1: cartilage is absent from bronchioles
B1: goblet cells are present in the trachea and bronchi but few or none in the smallest bronchioles
B1: smooth muscle is present in all three, forming a relatively larger part of the wall in bronchioles

questions.q: Which organism causes malaria?
questions.why: Plasmodium is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

questions.q: How does penicillin kill bacteria?
o: It stops cell wall synthesis, so cells burst
It blocks ribosomes in human cells
questions.why: Without strong walls, bacteria burst by osmosis as they grow.

questions.q: How is cholera transmitted?
o: Through water or food contaminated with faeces containing Vibrio cholerae
questions.why: Treatment of sewage and clean drinking water prevent it.

questions.q: Which pathogen causes tuberculosis (TB), and how is it usually transmitted?
o: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, in airborne droplets from an infected person
questions.why: TB is a bacterial disease spread when infected people cough or sneeze; it spreads more easily in overcrowded housing.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics not effective against HIV?
o: HIV is too small for antibiotics to reach
HIV has a thick cell wall that antibiotics cannot penetrate
Viruses have no cell walls, ribosomes or metabolism of their own for antibiotics to target; they use the host cell's machinery
questions.why: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures or processes such as cell wall synthesis or bacterial ribosomes; a virus has none of these to disrupt.

long.q: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
scheme: B1: a random mutation gives a bacterium resistance (e.g. a gene for an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic)
B1: when the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria survive and non-resistant ones die (selection pressure)
B1: resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on the allele, also by horizontal gene transfer on plasmids

long.q: Name the pathogen that causes cholera and explain how cholera is transmitted.
scheme: B1: Vibrio cholerae, a bacterium
B1: it is spread by drinking water or eating food contaminated with faeces from an infected person
B1: most likely where sanitation is poor and drinking water is not treated or sewage not disposed of safely

long.q: Describe how malaria is transmitted and explain why it is difficult to control.
scheme: B1: caused by Plasmodium (a protoctist), transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito as a vector
B1: the mosquito takes up gametes in the blood of an infected person and injects the parasite with saliva when it next feeds
B1: the parasite spends time inside liver cells and red blood cells, hidden from the immune system, and changes its antigens, so vaccines are hard to develop
B1: Plasmodium has become resistant to antimalarial drugs and mosquitoes to insecticides; mosquitoes breed in any standing water

long.q: Explain how infection with HIV leads to AIDS.
scheme: B1: HIV infects T helper lymphocytes
B1: it replicates inside them and destroys them, so their number falls over several years
B1: without T helper cells the immune system cannot respond well, so opportunistic infections (e.g. TB, pneumonia) develop: AIDS

long.q: Explain how penicillin kills bacteria and why it has no effect on viruses.
scheme: B1: penicillin inhibits the enzymes that form cross-links in the peptidoglycan cell wall of growing bacteria
B1: the wall is weakened, water enters by osmosis and the cell bursts (lysis)
B1: viruses have no cell wall (and no metabolism of their own), so there is nothing for penicillin to act on

questions.q: Which cells produce antibodies?
questions.why: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells.

questions.q: Passive immunity is…
questions.why: No memory cells are made, e.g. antibodies across the placenta.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by…
questions.why: They are identical and target one specific antigen.

questions.q: Why is the secondary immune response to a pathogen faster and larger than the primary response?
o: Antibodies from the first infection remain in the blood for life
The pathogen is weaker the second time
Plasma cells from the first infection keep dividing
Memory cells made during the first response recognise the antigen and divide rapidly
questions.why: Memory B and T cells persist after the primary response; on re-infection they quickly divide, producing many plasma cells and more antibody, often before symptoms appear.

questions.q: What is the main role of T helper cells in the immune response?
o: They produce antibodies against the antigen
They release cytokines that stimulate B cells to divide and become plasma cells, and activate other immune cells
They kill infected body cells directly
questions.why: T helper cells coordinate the response through cytokines; plasma cells make antibodies, T killer cells destroy infected cells, and phagocytes engulf pathogens.

long.q: Distinguish between active and passive immunity, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: active: the person's own immune system makes antibodies after meeting an antigen
B1: example: vaccination, or recovering from an infection
B1: passive: antibodies are given from outside; no memory cells form, so it is short-lived
B1: example: antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk, or an injection of antibodies

long.q: Describe how a neutrophil destroys a bacterium by phagocytosis.
scheme: B1: the neutrophil is attracted to the bacterium by chemicals (chemotaxis) and recognises it, e.g. by its antigens or attached antibodies
B1: the cell surface membrane extends around the bacterium and engulfs it into a vacuole (phagosome)
B1: lysosomes fuse with the phagosome
B1: hydrolytic enzymes (lysozymes) digest the bacterium

long.q: Describe the role of B lymphocytes in the primary immune response.
scheme: B1: an antigen binds to the B lymphocyte with complementary receptors (antibodies) on its surface (clonal selection)
B1: T helper cells release cytokines that stimulate this B cell
B1: the B cell divides by mitosis to form a clone (clonal expansion)
B1: some cells become plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of specific antibody
B1: others become memory cells, which remain in the blood

long.q: Describe the structure of an antibody molecule.
scheme: B1: four polypeptide chains: two heavy and two light (quaternary structure)
B1: held together by disulfide bonds
B1: a variable region at the tip of each arm forms an antigen-binding site complementary to one antigen
B1: a constant region (the same in all antibodies of a class) and a hinge region giving flexibility

long.q: Explain why the secondary immune response to an antigen is faster and greater than the primary response.
scheme: B1: memory cells made in the primary response remain in the body
B1: there are many of them, so the antigen is recognised quickly
B1: they divide rapidly into plasma cells, so a larger amount of antibody is made sooner, usually before symptoms develop

questions.q: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?
questions.why: Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm; link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix.

questions.q: What is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.why: Oxygen combines with electrons and H⁺ to form water.

questions.q: A respiratory quotient (RQ) near 0.7 suggests the substrate is…
questions.why: Carbohydrate 1.0, protein about 0.9, lipid about 0.7.

questions.q: In aerobic cellular respiration, where does the Krebs (citric acid) cycle take place?
questions.why: The matrix houses soluble enzymes for the link reaction and Krebs cycle; oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner membrane.

questions.q: In anaerobic conditions, yeast converts pyruvate to ethanol and CO₂. What is the main purpose of this?
o: To regenerate NAD so that glycolysis can continue
To store energy in ethanol for later use
questions.why: Without oxygen, reduced NAD cannot be reoxidised by the electron transport chain; reducing ethanal to ethanol reoxidises it, so glycolysis can keep making its net 2 ATP.

long.q: Explain how ATP is produced by oxidative phosphorylation.
scheme: B1: reduced NAD/FAD release electrons to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane
B1: energy from electron flow pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space
B1: H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis)
B1: driving ADP + Pi → ATP
B1: oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water

long.q: Describe the stages of glycolysis.
scheme: B1: glucose is phosphorylated using 2 ATP, forming hexose bisphosphate
B1: this splits into two molecules of triose phosphate
B1: each triose phosphate is oxidised by removal of hydrogen, reducing NAD
B1: pyruvate is formed, with 4 ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation (net gain of 2 ATP per glucose)

long.q: Explain why lactate is produced in mammalian muscle when oxygen is in short supply, and why much less ATP is made than in aerobic respiration.
scheme: B1: there is no oxygen to act as the final electron acceptor, so the electron transport chain stops and reduced NAD is not reoxidised there
B1: pyruvate is reduced to lactate (by lactate dehydrogenase), which reoxidises reduced NAD
B1: so NAD is available and glycolysis can continue
B1: only glycolysis makes ATP (net 2 per glucose); the link reaction, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation do not happen

long.q: Germinating seeds took in 25 cm³ of oxygen and gave out 18 cm³ of carbon dioxide in one hour. Calculate their respiratory quotient (RQ) and suggest which respiratory substrate they were using.
scheme: M1: RQ = volume of CO₂ given out ÷ volume of O₂ taken in
B1: lipid (RQ about 0.7)

long.q: Describe the link reaction and the Krebs cycle.
scheme: B1: pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix (by active transport)
B1: link reaction: pyruvate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated, reducing NAD, and the acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A
B1: the 2C acetyl group combines with 4C oxaloacetate to form 6C citrate
B1: citrate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated in steps, regenerating oxaloacetate
B1: each turn releases 2 CO₂ and makes reduced NAD, reduced FAD and one ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation

questions.q: Where does the light-dependent stage happen?
questions.why: Photosystems and the electron transport chain are in the thylakoids.

questions.q: Which enzyme fixes CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
questions.why: Rubisco combines CO₂ with RuBP.

questions.q: A limiting factor is…
o: the factor that controls the rate because it is in shortest supply
questions.why: Increasing it increases the rate until another factor limits.

questions.q: In the light-independent stage of photosynthesis (Calvin cycle), which enzyme fixes CO₂ to ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP)?
questions.why: RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase-oxygenase) catalyses the primary carbon fixation reaction yielding 3-PGA.

questions.q: A photosynthesising plant is suddenly placed in the dark. What happens to the concentrations of GP and RuBP in its chloroplasts?
questions.why: Without light there is no ATP or reduced NADP to reduce GP to triose phosphate, so GP builds up; RuBP is still used in fixing CO₂ but cannot be regenerated, so it falls.

long.q: Describe the light-independent stage of photosynthesis (the Calvin cycle).
scheme: B1: CO₂ combines with RuBP, catalysed by rubisco
B1: forming two molecules of GP
B1: GP reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and reduced NADP
B1: most TP regenerates RuBP, using ATP

long.q: Describe non-cyclic photophosphorylation.
scheme: B1: light absorbed by photosystem II excites electrons to a higher energy level, and they leave the chlorophyll
B1: the electrons pass along an electron transport chain in the thylakoid membrane, and the energy released pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space
B1: H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase, making ATP (chemiosmosis)
B1: photolysis of water replaces the electrons lost from PSII, releasing H⁺ and oxygen
B1: electrons are re-excited in photosystem I and, with H⁺, reduce NADP

long.q: A plant is kept at a high light intensity with 0.04% carbon dioxide. Increasing the light intensity further does not increase its rate of photosynthesis. Explain why, and suggest what change would increase the rate.
scheme: B1: light intensity is no longer the limiting factor
B1: another factor, most likely carbon dioxide concentration (or temperature), is now limiting the rate
B1: increasing the CO₂ concentration (e.g. to 0.1%) would increase the rate, until another factor becomes limiting

long.q: In paper chromatography of a leaf extract the solvent front moved 8.0 cm from the origin and one pigment spot moved 3.6 cm. Calculate the Rf value of the pigment and suggest why leaves contain several different pigments.
scheme: M1: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front
B1: different pigments absorb different wavelengths of light, so a wider range of wavelengths can be used for photosynthesis

long.q: Explain how the structure of a chloroplast is adapted for photosynthesis.
scheme: B1: many thylakoid membranes stacked into grana give a large surface area for photosystems, electron carriers and ATP synthase
B1: the small thylakoid space allows a steep H⁺ gradient to build up quickly
B1: the stroma contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle (e.g. rubisco), close to where ATP and reduced NADP are made
B1: the chloroplast has its own DNA and 70S ribosomes, so it can make some of its own proteins

questions.q: Which hormone increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
questions.why: ADH inserts aquaporins, making urine more concentrated.

questions.q: Homeostasis mainly works by…
questions.why: A change triggers a response that reverses it.

questions.q: Guard cells open stomata by…
o: taking in K⁺, lowering water potential, then water enters and they swell
questions.why: Turgid guard cells bend apart because of uneven wall thickness.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT normally found in the glomerular filtrate of a healthy kidney?
questions.why: Plasma proteins are too large to pass through the basement membrane during ultrafiltration; small molecules such as glucose, urea and ions pass into the filtrate.

questions.q: How does glucagon raise blood glucose concentration?
o: It increases the uptake of glucose by muscle cells
It converts glucose into glycogen in liver cells
It is released by β cells and acts directly on glycogen
It binds to receptors on liver cells and, via the second messenger cAMP, activates enzymes for glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis
questions.why: Glucagon from α cells cannot enter the cell; binding to its receptor starts a cAMP signalling cascade that activates enzymes breaking down glycogen and making glucose from other compounds.

long.q: Explain how blood glucose concentration is lowered after a meal.
scheme: B1: β cells in the islets of Langerhans detect the rise and secrete insulin
B1: insulin binds to receptors on liver and muscle cells
B1: more glucose transporters (GLUT4) in membranes, so more glucose uptake
B1: glucose converted to glycogen (glycogenesis)
B1: negative feedback

long.q: Describe how ultrafiltration occurs in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule.
scheme: B1: the afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, so the blood in the glomerulus is at high hydrostatic pressure
B1: fluid is forced out through gaps in the capillary endothelium
B1: the basement membrane acts as the filter, with podocytes on the capsule wall leaving slits for the filtrate to pass
B1: small molecules (water, glucose, urea, ions) pass into the filtrate; blood cells and large plasma proteins stay in the blood

long.q: Explain how ADH reduces the volume of urine when the water potential of the blood falls.
scheme: B1: osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in water potential
B1: more ADH is released from the posterior pituitary gland into the blood
B1: ADH binds to receptors on cells of the collecting duct (and distal convoluted tubule)
B1: vesicles containing aquaporins fuse with the cell surface membrane, so it becomes more permeable to water
B1: more water is reabsorbed by osmosis into the medulla, which has a low water potential, so a small volume of concentrated urine forms

long.q: Explain how glucose is reabsorbed from the filtrate in the proximal convoluted tubule.
scheme: B1: Na⁺/K⁺ pumps in the basal membrane actively move Na⁺ out of the tubule cells into the blood, using ATP
B1: this keeps the Na⁺ concentration in the cells low
B1: Na⁺ diffuses into the cells from the filtrate through cotransporter proteins, carrying glucose with it
B1: glucose then moves into the blood by facilitated diffusion; microvilli and many mitochondria make this fast

long.q: Explain how abscisic acid causes stomata to close when a plant is short of water.
scheme: B1: abscisic acid binds to receptors on the guard cell membranes
B1: calcium ions enter the cytoplasm and act as a second messenger
B1: potassium ions leave the guard cells (and proton pumping stops)
B1: the water potential in the guard cells rises, so water leaves by osmosis
B1: the guard cells lose turgor and become flaccid, closing the stoma and reducing water loss

questions.q: What causes the depolarisation in an action potential?
o: Na⁺ rushing in through voltage-gated channels
questions.why: Repolarisation then follows as K⁺ leaves.

questions.q: Myelination speeds up conduction by…
o: saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
questions.why: Action potentials jump from node to node.

questions.q: Which plant hormone stimulates stomatal closure in drought?
questions.why: ABA triggers K⁺ loss from guard cells.

questions.q: What maintains the resting potential of a neurone at about −70 mV?
o: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane is more permeable to K⁺, which diffuses out
Acetylcholine binds to the axon membrane
questions.why: More positive charge leaves than enters through the pump, and K⁺ leaking out through open channels leaves the inside negative relative to the outside.

questions.q: Why can a nerve impulse cross a synapse in one direction only?
o: Neurotransmitter is released only from the presynaptic neurone, and receptors are only on the postsynaptic membrane
The synaptic cleft is too wide for ions to cross backwards
Myelin blocks transmission in the other direction
Acetylcholinesterase is found only in the presynaptic knob
questions.why: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are in the presynaptic knob and the receptors are on the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal can only pass from pre- to postsynaptic neurone.

long.q: Explain how a nerve impulse is transmitted across a cholinergic synapse.
scheme: B1: action potential arrives; Ca²⁺ channels open and Ca²⁺ enters the presynaptic knob
B1: vesicles fuse and release acetylcholine by exocytosis
B1: ACh diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
B1: Na⁺ channels open, depolarising the membrane
B1: acetylcholinesterase breaks down ACh

long.q: Explain how the resting potential of a neurone is maintained.
scheme: B1: sodium–potassium pumps actively transport 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, using ATP
B1: the membrane is more permeable to K⁺ than to Na⁺ because more K⁺ channels are open
B1: so K⁺ diffuses out faster than Na⁺ diffuses in
B1: the inside is left negative compared with the outside, at about −70 mV

long.q: Explain how myelination increases the speed of conduction of a nerve impulse.
scheme: B1: the myelin sheath is an electrical insulator, so ions cannot move across the membrane where it is present
B1: depolarisation can only happen at the nodes of Ranvier, the gaps in the sheath
B1: local circuits run from node to node, so the impulse jumps between them (saltatory conduction)

long.q: Describe how the arrival of an action potential at a skeletal muscle fibre leads to contraction.
scheme: B1: depolarisation spreads along the T-tubules, causing the sarcoplasmic reticulum to release Ca²⁺
B1: Ca²⁺ binds to troponin, moving tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin
B1: myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges
B1: the heads tilt (power stroke), pulling the actin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere, which shortens; ADP and Pi are released
B1: ATP binds, the myosin head detaches, and hydrolysis of ATP returns the head to its original position to bind again

long.q: Explain how gibberellin brings about the germination of a barley seed.
scheme: B1: the seed absorbs water and the embryo produces gibberellin
B1: gibberellin causes the breakdown of DELLA proteins, which were inhibiting a transcription factor
B1: so the gene for amylase is transcribed in the aleurone layer
B1: amylase hydrolyses starch in the endosperm to maltose / glucose, which the embryo uses for respiration and growth

questions.q: Crossing over happens in…
questions.why: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange sections.

questions.q: A chi-squared test compares…
questions.why: It tests whether differences from the expected ratio are due to chance.

questions.q: Epistasis is…
o: one gene affecting the expression of another gene
questions.why: It changes expected dihybrid ratios.

questions.q: A plant heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb) is crossed with a plant that is aabb. What is the expected phenotypic ratio of the offspring?
questions.why: The AaBb parent makes four gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab) in equal numbers by independent assortment; the aabb parent only gives ab, so each gamete type gives a different phenotype.

questions.q: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A carrier woman (XᴴXʰ) and an unaffected man (XᴴY) have a son. What is the probability that the son has haemophilia?
questions.why: A son gets Y from his father and one of his mother's two X chromosomes, so there is a 1 in 2 chance he inherits Xʰ. 1/4 is the chance that any child is an affected son.

long.q: In a dihybrid cross between two plants heterozygous for both genes (AaBb × AaBb), state the expected phenotypic ratio and explain what a significantly different result could suggest.
scheme: B1: genes on different chromosomes assort independently
B1: a different ratio may suggest linkage (genes on the same chromosome)
B1: test with chi-squared

long.q: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation produce genetic variation.
scheme: B1: crossing over in prophase I: non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange sections, giving new combinations of alleles
B1: independent assortment of homologous pairs at metaphase I
B1: independent assortment of chromatids at metaphase II
B1: random fertilisation: any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete

long.q: In a test cross the expected ratio was 1 : 1. Of 100 offspring, 56 had one phenotype and 44 the other. Calculate χ² and say what it shows. The critical value for 1 degree of freedom at p = 0.05 is 3.84.
scheme: M1: expected numbers are 50 and 50
B1: 1.44 is less than 3.84, so the difference is not significant; it is due to chance and the results fit a 1 : 1 ratio

long.q: Haemophilia is caused by a recessive allele on the X chromosome. A woman who is a carrier has children with a man who does not have haemophilia. Using Xᴴ and Xʰ, show the genotypes of the parents, their gametes and the possible offspring, and state the probability that their next child will be a son with haemophilia.
scheme: B1: parents' genotypes: woman XᴴXʰ, man XᴴY
B1: gametes: Xᴴ and Xʰ from the woman; Xᴴ and Y from the man
B1: offspring: XᴴXᴴ, XᴴXʰ, XᴴY, XʰY (unaffected girl, carrier girl, unaffected boy, boy with haemophilia)
B1: probability of a son with haemophilia = 1 in 4 (0.25)

long.q: Explain how the lac operon allows the bacterium E. coli to make β-galactosidase only when lactose is present.
scheme: B1: a regulatory gene codes for a repressor protein
B1: without lactose, the repressor binds to the operator, so RNA polymerase cannot bind to the promoter and the structural genes are not transcribed
B1: when lactose is present it binds to the repressor, changing its shape
B1: the repressor can no longer bind to the operator
B1: RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and the structural genes (lacZ, lacY) are transcribed, so β-galactosidase and lactose permease are made

questions.q: The Hardy–Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1. What is 2pq?
questions.why: p² = AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa.

questions.q: Genetic drift has the largest effect in…
questions.why: Chance changes in allele frequency matter more when numbers are small.

questions.q: What is genetic drift?
o: Random changes in allele frequency, strongest in small populations
questions.why: The founder effect and bottlenecks are examples.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 16% of individuals show the recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of heterozygotes?
questions.why: q² = 0.16, so q = 0.4 and p = 0.6; heterozygotes = 2pq = 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. 0.36 is p² and 0.84 is everyone with the dominant phenotype.

questions.q: Which sequence describes allopatric speciation?
o: Mutation in one individual immediately produces a new species
Populations are separated by a geographical barrier; different selection pressures and genetic drift change their gene pools until they can no longer interbreed
Populations in the same area become reproductively isolated by behavioural changes
Individuals acquire useful characteristics during their lives and pass them on
questions.why: Allopatric speciation needs geographical isolation first; reproductive isolation in the same area is sympatric speciation, and passing on acquired characteristics is not how evolution works.

long.q: In a population, 9% of individuals show a recessive phenotype. Use the Hardy–Weinberg principle to calculate the proportion of the population that is heterozygous.
Explain how a new species can arise by allopatric speciation.
scheme: B1: a population is divided by a geographical barrier, e.g. a mountain range, river or sea
B1: there is no gene flow between the two populations
B1: different selection pressures, different mutations and genetic drift change the allele frequencies in each
B1: eventually the populations are reproductively isolated: they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring

long.q: Explain the difference between stabilising selection and directional selection, giving an example of each.
scheme: B1: stabilising selection favours the average phenotype and acts against both extremes, so the mean stays the same and variation decreases
B1: example, e.g. human birth mass: very small and very large babies have lower survival
B1: directional selection favours one extreme phenotype, usually after the environment changes, so the mean shifts in that direction
B1: example, e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria, or darker peppered moths in polluted areas

long.q: The leaf lengths of two populations of a plant were compared. Population 1: mean 12.0 mm, standard deviation 2.0 mm, n = 10. Population 2: mean 10.0 mm, standard deviation 1.5 mm, n = 10. Use t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) ÷ √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) to calculate t and say what it shows. The critical value at p = 0.05 for 18 degrees of freedom is 2.10.
scheme: B1: 2.53 is greater than 2.10, so the difference in mean leaf length is significant (not due to chance); reject the null hypothesis

long.q: Describe how selective breeding could be used to increase the milk yield of a herd of dairy cattle.
scheme: B1: select the cows with the highest milk yield
B1: select bulls whose mothers or daughters had high milk yields (bulls cannot be measured directly)
B1: breed these together (e.g. by artificial insemination) and select the highest-yielding offspring
B1: repeat over many generations, so alleles for high yield become more frequent

questions.q: Simpson's index of diversity is higher when…
o: there are many species with similar numbers
questions.why: Diversity includes both richness and evenness.

questions.q: Which are the three domains?
questions.why: Domains are the highest rank in classification.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of taxonomic ranks, largest first?
o: Kingdom, domain, class, phylum, order, genus, family, species
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species
Species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom, domain
Domain, phylum, kingdom, class, family, order, genus, species
questions.why: There are three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya.

questions.q: A sample contains 10 individuals of species A, 6 of species B and 4 of species C. Using D = 1 − Σ(n/N)², what is Simpson's index of diversity?
questions.why: N = 20, so Σ(n/N)² = 0.5² + 0.3² + 0.2² = 0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.38, and D = 1 − 0.38 = 0.62. 0.38 is the result if you forget to subtract from 1.

questions.q: Why are viruses not placed in any of the three domains?
o: They are too small to see with a light microscope
They are not made of cells and cannot carry out metabolism or reproduce outside a host cell
questions.why: The domains classify cellular organisms; viruses are acellular, so they are classified separately by features such as their nucleic acid type (DNA or RNA).

long.q: A sample from a pond contained three species: 10 individuals of species A, 6 of species B and 4 of species C. Calculate Simpson's index of diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)².
40 woodlice were caught, marked and released. A week later 50 were caught, of which 8 were marked. Estimate the population size, and state one assumption the method makes.
scheme: M1: N = (number in first sample × number in second sample) ÷ number marked in second sample = (40 × 50) ÷ 8
B1: assumption, e.g. marked individuals mix randomly with the population, marks are not lost and do not affect survival, or no births, deaths or migration between samples

long.q: Name the three domains of living organisms and state two ways in which organisms in the Archaea differ from those in the Bacteria.
scheme: B1: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya
B1: Archaea have no peptidoglycan in their cell walls
B1: Archaea have different membrane lipids (ether-linked), or RNA polymerase / ribosomal RNA more like that of eukaryotes

long.q: Explain how seed banks and captive breeding programmes in zoos help to conserve endangered species.
scheme: B1: seed banks dry seeds and store them at low temperature (about −20 °C), so they stay viable for a long time
B1: they hold seeds from many individuals, conserving genetic diversity, and seeds can be grown to restore populations
B1: zoos breed endangered animals in captivity, using records (studbooks), exchange between zoos or IVF / embryo transfer to avoid inbreeding
B1: offspring can be reintroduced to the wild, and zoos also support education and research

long.q: Describe how you would use quadrats to estimate the number of daisy plants in a field.
scheme: B1: mark out the field as a grid and use random numbers to choose coordinates, so sampling is random
B1: place a quadrat of known area (e.g. 1 m²) at each coordinate and count the daisy plants inside
B1: use a large number of quadrats (e.g. at least 20) and calculate the mean number per quadrat
B1: estimate = mean number per quadrat × (area of field ÷ area of one quadrat)

questions.q: What does PCR do?
o: Makes many copies of a DNA sequence
questions.why: Cycles of denaturing, annealing primers and extending with Taq polymerase.

questions.q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by…
questions.why: Negatively charged DNA moves towards the anode; small fragments travel faster.

questions.q: What do restriction enzymes do?
o: Cut DNA at specific base sequences
questions.why: DNA ligase joins fragments; sticky ends help them pair.

questions.q: Why is the same restriction enzyme used to cut both the plasmid and the DNA containing the gene to be inserted?
o: So that both pieces of DNA are the same length
So that the gene is copied many times
So that both have complementary sticky ends that base-pair, before DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones
So that the plasmid cannot be taken up by bacteria
questions.why: One restriction enzyme leaves matching single-stranded overhangs on both molecules, so the gene and plasmid base-pair by hydrogen bonding and ligase then seals them.

questions.q: To make human insulin in bacteria, the gene is usually made from insulin mRNA using reverse transcriptase rather than cut from human chromosomal DNA. Why?
o: The cDNA made from mRNA has no introns, and bacteria cannot remove introns
Reverse transcriptase also adds a promoter that bacteria recognise
Bacteria can only use RNA, not DNA
questions.why: Mature mRNA has already been spliced, so cDNA copied from it codes for insulin with no introns; bacteria have no splicing machinery to remove them from a eukaryotic gene.

long.q: Describe how PCR is used to amplify a sample of DNA.
scheme: B1: heated to about 95 °C to separate the strands
B1: cooled to about 55 °C so primers anneal
B1: heated to about 72 °C; Taq polymerase extends the strands
B1: cycle repeated, doubling the DNA each time

long.q: Describe how bacteria can be genetically modified to produce human insulin.
scheme: B1: mRNA for insulin is extracted from pancreatic β cells and reverse transcriptase makes cDNA, which has no introns
B1: a plasmid is cut with a restriction enzyme, leaving sticky ends complementary to sticky ends added to the gene
B1: DNA ligase joins the gene into the plasmid, with a promoter so it is expressed, forming recombinant DNA

long.q: Explain how gel electrophoresis separates fragments of DNA.
scheme: B1: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate groups
B1: when a voltage is applied, the fragments move through the agarose gel towards the positive electrode (anode)
B1: smaller fragments move faster through the gel, so they travel further in the same time

long.q: Outline how gene therapy could be used to treat an inherited condition caused by a recessive allele, and suggest one problem with it.
scheme: B1: a normal (dominant) allele of the gene is inserted into the patient's cells
B1: using a vector, e.g. a virus (adenovirus, lentivirus) or a liposome
B1: usually somatic cells, so the change is not passed to children (germ-line therapy is not permitted in humans in most countries)
B1: problem, e.g. an immune response to the vector, the gene inserting in a place that causes cancer, or the effect being temporary so treatment must be repeated

long.q: Discuss the benefits and concerns of growing a crop that has been genetically modified to be resistant to a herbicide.
scheme: B1: benefit: the field can be sprayed so the weeds die and the crop survives, reducing competition
B1: benefit: higher yields, and possibly fewer herbicide applications
B1: concern: the gene could pass to wild relatives by pollen, producing herbicide-resistant weeds, or biodiversity on farmland falls as weeds are removed
B1: concern: farmers depend on buying seed and herbicide from one company each year, which may disadvantage poorer farmers
